clue.text: Vain candidate's girl with sailor seen in Private Eye

indicators.note: something seen in a place sits inside it, so the girl and sailor go within the outer letters

parts.note: the magazine's editorial voice, which speaks of itself as 'we'
a girl's name
AB, able-bodied seaman

explanation.surface: A gossip item about a self-regarding politician's girlfriend and her sailor, as reported in Private Eye.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the inner girl-plus-sailor are clear; reading Private Eye as WE, the paper's editorial 'we', is the least certain step of this parse.
explanation.definitionFit: A wannabe is a would-be who aspires in vain to something, like a hopeful candidate with no real chance.

clue.text: Hip and seat switched — and nuts

indicators.note: letters that are switched around are moved into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A body swapped round at hip and seat, as if after a botched operation, has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'and' joins the two words of fodder; the second, after the dash, joins wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Going apeshit is vulgar slang for becoming wildly crazy or furious, the same sense as being nuts.

clue.text: Only deviously securing Brown's end is material

indicators.note: acting deviously means taking a crooked route, so the letters go out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: last letter of Brown, Gordon Brown then Chancellor

explanation.surface: A dig at Gordon Brown, the Chancellor, whose aim is only deviously secured.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown's last letter joins the four letters of Only before the shuffle; 'securing' just brings that letter in, since it ends up at one end rather than inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Nylon is a synthetic fabric, a manufactured material used for clothing, stockings and rope.

clue.text: Fall from grace, Labour's leader must go, the arse!

indicators.note: what must go is removed from the word it sits in

parts.note: to backslide is to lapse back into sin

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of Labour is meant

parts.note: first letter of Labour

explanation.surface: A party member rages at a disgraced Labour leader who must resign.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour's leader looks like Tony Blair himself; it is only the letter L, taken out of the backslider.
explanation.definitionFit: The backside is the bottom or buttocks, which is what 'the arse' means in British slang.

clue.text: Codicils, one with date written by bum lawyer on the outside

indicators.note: a word placed on the outside wraps around another one

parts.note: one as the article a
D is a standard abbreviation for date
a district attorney, an American prosecutor
the end is the backside, as in 'rear end'

explanation.surface: Extra clauses in a will, dated and drafted by a useless lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum lawyer' reads as a hopeless lawyer, but bum is its own piece, the end, with the lawyer's letters around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Addenda are additions attached to a document, as codicils are supplements added to a will.

clue.text: Casual habit of Di's, getting involved with men

indicators.note: things getting involved with each other are tangled up and mixed together

parts.note: Di, Princess Diana, with her possessive s
taken as written

explanation.surface: Gossip about Princess Diana's casual habit of getting involved with men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' reads as a pattern of behaviour; it is clothing, as in a nun's habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Denims are jeans or other denim clothes, informal wear, and a habit is an old word for dress.

clue.text: (see 14ac.)
Lives over German surrounded by Polish loathing

indicators.note: letters surrounded by a word sit inside it

parts.note: to dust is to polish furniture
to live is to exist, so 'lives' is 'is'
G, the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: Someone living above a German neighbour, surrounded by Polish hatred.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts one piece above, so before, the next. The capital P makes Polish a nationality, but it is the housework verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Disgust is strong revulsion, a near synonym for loathing.

clue.text: What Labour want: to stagger on, etc. pathetically with no one doing a U-turn

parts.note: to reel is to stagger

indicators.note: a U-turn faces the other way, so the letters run backwards
something done pathetically is botched, so these letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A jibe that New Labour just staggers on pathetically, with nobody making a policy U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With no one doing a U-turn' sounds like political commentary, but it means reverse the letters of no plus one.
explanation.definitionFit: Any governing party wants to be voted back in at the next election, which is re-election.

clue.text: Unintentionally responsible for a leak about Northern Ireland uniting with America, say?

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, as in about-face, so the letters face the other way

parts.note: NI is the standard abbreviation for Northern Ireland
America is an example of a continent, as 'say' signals

explanation.surface: A political leak blamed on talks about Northern Ireland and the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A leak' reads as a leaked document; it is a bodily leak, which makes the definition a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone incontinent cannot control their bladder, so a leak happens without them meaning it.

clue.text: Dismiss French novelist pushing out pair

indicators.note: something pushed out is forced away, so those letters leave the word

parts.note: Marcel Proust, author of In Search of Lost Time
pr is the standard abbreviation for pair

explanation.surface: A French writer is sacked for elbowing out a couple of colleagues.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust is to force someone out of a post, which is to dismiss them.

clue.text: Mo turns and leaves US movie star — that's gratitude for you!

indicators.note: something that turns round faces the opposite way, so its letters run backwards
what leaves a word is no longer part of it

parts.note: taken as written
Tom Hanks, the American film actor

explanation.surface: Mo Mowlam turns her back and walks out on a Hollywood star, and a sarcastic cry follows.
explanation.walkthrough: Mo suggests Mo Mowlam, the Labour minister; here it is just two letters, turned round and removed from the actor's full name.
explanation.definitionFit: Thanks is the word for expressing gratitude, said as a short exclamation.

clue.text: Play the Queen at "PM I dismissed" in prize environment

indicators.note: an environment surrounds whatever lives in it, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: a cup is a trophy, a prize

indicators.note: a dismissed team is scattered, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A theatrical send-up of the Queen dismissing her Prime Minister at an awards ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Queen' looks like the monarch; queen is also slang for an effeminate gay man, and to play one is to act camply.
explanation.definitionFit: To camp it up is to behave in a flamboyant, exaggerated, theatrical way, as a stage queen would.

clue.text: (& 7dn.) Madonna tried to lie about being pissed

indicators.note: about can mean all around, in disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The pop star Madonna fibbed about having been drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: This is Private Eye's own famous euphemism for a public figure who is drunk, used to dodge libel suits.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a polite cover for intoxication, and pissed is British slang for drunk.

clue.text: Go quickly through conductor Dicky

parts.note: Sir Simon Rattle, the British orchestral conductor
dicky is British slang for poorly or unsound, and off means unwell or gone bad

explanation.surface: A conductor called Dicky races through the score.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a name; it is British slang, as in a dicky heart.
explanation.definitionFit: To rattle off a list or speech is to recite it rapidly, getting through it at speed.

clue.text: Bollocks act amazingly when given a twirl

indicators.note: a twirl spins something round so it faces the other way

parts.note: to stun is to amaze

explanation.surface: A crude dismissal of a dancer's routine that only impresses when it spins.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are vulgar exclamations of disbelief meaning nonsense, and both are also slang for testicles.

clue.text: Shag and peak with bottle-top

parts.note: both are crude slang for having sex
a cap is the top or crowning point, as of a mountain

explanation.surface: A sex romp on a mountain summit, celebrated with a bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: A screw cap is a threaded lid that twists onto the neck of a bottle to close it.

clue.text: Prescott: firstly an arse, then "tosser"

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the buttocks, the word's original slang sense
second meaning: a fool or idiot, the later sense

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at John Prescott, Labour's deputy prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firstly ... then' gives the history of the word: it meant the backside before it meant a fool, and Prescott is the one being called it.
explanation.definitionFit: Prat is old slang for the buttocks and modern British slang for an idiot, so both insults fit.

clue.text: Finally, Mr Bean needs to swallow stimulant to beat off

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside, so one piece goes into the others
finally points to the closing letter of the next word only

parts.note: last letter of Mr
a pulse is an edible bean, pea or lentil
E is ecstasy, the stimulant drug

explanation.surface: Rowan Atkinson's Mr Bean pops a pill before a solo sex act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat off' tempts as the smutty sense; it is the military one, to drive back an attack. Mr Bean is split: Mr gives a letter, Bean a legume.
explanation.definitionFit: To repulse an enemy or attack is to drive it back, which is to beat it off.

clue.text: Bill: Blair ultimately involved in crucial cock-up

indicators.note: a cock-up is a mess, so these letters are muddled into a new order
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of Blair
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bill Clinton, with Tony Blair, mixed up in a crucial blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill reads as Clinton, Blair's ally; it is a printed notice. A cock-up is British slang for a botched job.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular is a printed notice or leaflet handed out widely, much as a bill is a posted notice.

clue.text: Tony Blair's limits apparent in answer: "Issue a disclaimer!"

indicators.note: something apparent in another thing is seen inside it

parts.note: to react is to answer or respond

indicators.note: the limits of something are its two outer edges, so only first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the name

explanation.surface: Tony Blair's limitations show in his reply, and he is told to put out a denial.
explanation.definitionFit: To retract a statement is to withdraw it, formally disowning what was said, which is issuing a disclaimer.

clue.text: Ready to show where the wanker came?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: available, prepared, as in having cash to hand
second meaning: a crude joke about where a masturbator ejaculates

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second half as a joke reading of the everyday phrase, taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Having something in hand means it is under control and available for use, so it is ready.

clue.text: Posh's quality enrolled nurse comes between the unhappy couple

indicators.note: something that comes between others is placed in the middle of them
an unhappy pair is out of sorts, so these letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written
EN, an enrolled nurse

explanation.surface: Posh Spice's marriage to David Beckham is under strain as a nurse comes between them.
explanation.walkthrough: Posh is Victoria Beckham's Spice Girls nickname, but here it is just the adjective for grand and wealthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Opulence is lavish wealth and luxury, the defining quality of anything posh.

clue.text: Swear Spielberg film with implausible ending is rather feeble

parts.note: to eff is to swear, from the F-word, as in 'eff and blind'
E.T., Steven Spielberg's film about an alien

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its last letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: last letter of implausible

explanation.surface: Cursing at a Spielberg film whose unlikely ending is weak.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete means weak, ineffectual and lacking vigour, so it describes something rather feeble.

clue.text: One who got a blast from the chair, reportedly, brother

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so it is the sound that counts

parts.words: One who got a blast from the chair
parts.note: someone who fried in the electric chair

explanation.surface: A monk who was executed in the electric chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A blast from the chair' sounds like a reprimand from whoever chairs a meeting; it is a jolt from the electric chair.
explanation.definitionFit: A friar is a member of a religious order, addressed as Brother.

clue.text: Too political, sovereign's contribution

indicators.note: a contribution is a part of a whole, so the letters are a part of the words

parts.note: the end of political runs into the start of sovereign's

explanation.surface: A complaint that the monarch's speech is too political.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too' opens the clue as an adverb of excess; it is the definition, in its other sense of 'as well'.
explanation.definitionFit: Also and too are synonyms, both meaning in addition.

clue.text: Let-down Northern relative cried out with orgasm

indicators.note: something cried out is heard spoken, so its sound is what is kept

parts.note: auntie, as said with the short Northern English a
a climax is an orgasm

explanation.surface: A disappointing encounter with a Northern relative who shouted out at the climax.
explanation.walkthrough: Northern says how the relative is pronounced: in the North of England auntie is said with a short a.
explanation.definitionFit: An anticlimax is a disappointing end after rising expectations, which is a let-down.

clue.text: For each female DIY fiasco there's an act of infidelity

parts.note: per means for each, as in per head

indicators.note: a fiasco is a shambles, so these letters end up in a mess

parts.note: F, the abbreviation for female
taken as written

explanation.surface: Every woman's botched home improvement leads her into an affair.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfidy is treachery or breach of faith, so a betrayal of a partner counts as an instance of it.

clue.text: "Fairies", according to hawks securing Iran without one

indicators.note: securing something means holding it fast inside

parts.note: to hawk is to clear the throat and spit

indicators.note: without means lacking, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
one as the article an

explanation.surface: Warmongering hawks sneer at doves as fairies while they hold Iran in their grip.
explanation.walkthrough: Hawks are the war party in the surface; here it is the verb, to cough and spit.
explanation.definitionFit: Fairies are supernatural beings, and spirits is a general word for such sprites.
